title: Enzyme-level catalysts on request for arbitrary reactions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable method for turning a requested chemical transformation into a practical catalyst with the efficiency and selectivity of evolved enzymes. A chemist would specify the starting materials, desired bond changes and operating conditions; the method would produce a catalyst that accelerates the intended reaction while suppressing unwanted products. Its intended scope includes transformations for which nature provides no useful enzyme starting point. This is a general design capability, extending beyond successful designs for individual model reactions.

The supplied studies illustrate a technical basis for this goal: model a catalytic active site and build a protein environment that makes it work. Listov and colleagues demonstrated designed catalysts for Kemp elimination, a model proton-abstraction reaction. Kim, Woodbury, Ahern and colleagues demonstrated zinc-dependent ester hydrolases using RFdiffusion2 and PLACER, with active-site configurations derived from quantum chemistry calculations. These achievements connect computational designs to measured catalytic activity, but do not establish that a user can request an arbitrary reaction and reliably obtain a suitable catalyst.

significance.text: Natural enzymes combine high activity with selectivity for particular reactions. Extending those qualities to reliably designed catalysts for user-chosen transformations could make catalysis substantially more programmable. The direct consequence would be access to catalysts and reaction steps that chemists cannot currently obtain through the demonstrated workflows. The revolutionary significance is an inference from that proposed capability: it could expand synthetic routes and reduce dependence on finding a suitable existing enzyme before engineering can begin.

Conditional impact synthesis: manufacturing could change where the availability of an efficient, selective catalyst is the limiting factor. New catalysts might enable alternative routes or replace particular existing processes, including some that use precious metals. Such changes would depend on reaction-specific economics, catalyst lifetime, substrate compatibility, operating conditions and product recovery. High catalytic activity in a laboratory assay alone does not establish industrial adoption or superiority to an incumbent process.

Conditional application synthesis: mild nitrogen fixation, methane oxidation and selective late-stage C–H editing are possible targets for a general catalyst designer. None is demonstrated by the supplied studies. Each requires its own successful chemistry and practical performance, and each could in principle be solved through a specialized catalyst without achieving a general design method. The analogy to programming therefore has a boundary: specifying a desired transformation would not itself establish that the chemistry is feasible under the requested conditions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied evidence is reliable generalization from selected successful reactions to unfamiliar transformations, especially difficult bond changes without a useful natural enzyme starting point. Neither highlighted study demonstrates a method that consistently returns catalysts matching evolved enzymes in efficiency and selectivity under process conditions. That is a limitation of what these studies establish; the supplied record does not support a categorical claim that the broader capability remained unavailable throughout the field as of 1 November 2026.

A central scientific barrier is translating an idealized catalytic arrangement into a protein that actually supports rapid chemistry. Listov and colleagues identify improved modelling of theoretical active sites, or theozymes, as a route toward programmable biocatalysis. The metallohydrolase study provides a complementary demonstration of generating active proteins from calculated catalytic configurations. Together these results motivate the broader goal, while leaving unresolved how predictably such approaches transfer across reaction mechanisms, substrates and catalytic requirements.

Engineering synthesis: a general method would need to coordinate substrate binding, the geometry and chemical environment of catalytic groups, stabilization of the relevant reaction pathway, and product release. It would also need to favor the desired product over competing reactions and remain active under the intended temperature, pH, solvent and substrate concentrations. For metal-dependent catalysts, the required metal environment must function reliably as part of the complete catalyst. These are proposed dimensions of the unsolved engineering problem, not failures individually established for every catalyst in the supplied studies.

A further barrier is predictable design efficiency. Successful computational design can still involve experimental screening and redesign: the Listov workflow did so without a directed-evolution campaign, and the zinc-hydrolase study tested two sets of 96 designs. A convincing on-request capability would need to make the number of designs tested, the iteration burden and the frequency of success predictable across new reaction requests.

current_state.text: In the study published online on 18 June 2025, Listov and colleagues designed Kemp eliminases. Des27.7 reached a catalytic efficiency, kcat/KM, of 12,700 M−1 s−1 and a turnover rate, kcat, of approximately 2.8 s−1; the results text gives 2.85 s−1. A further designed variant, Phe113Leu, reached 123,000 M−1 s−1 and 30 s−1. The latter turnover value is 30 s−1, rather than greater than 30 s−1. These results concern Kemp elimination, a model base-catalysed proton-abstraction reaction.

The Listov workflow included experimental screening and computational redesign without a directed-evolution campaign. Consequently, avoiding directed evolution should not be read as avoiding experimental testing or iterative optimization. The paper's introductory description of natural-level proficiency for non-natural reactions as a longstanding difficulty provides historical context; its subsequent results demonstrate progress on that challenge for the tested reaction. The paper also cites median natural-enzyme values of roughly 10^5 M−1 s−1 for kcat/KM and 10 s−1 for kcat. Those aggregate reference values do not establish that every natural enzyme or every practical catalytic task should meet the same thresholds.

In the study published online on 3 December 2025 and appearing in Nature volume 649 in 2026, Donghyo Kim, Seth M. Woodbury, Woody Ahern and colleagues, including David Baker, designed zinc ester hydrolases. The best of an initial 96 designs reached kcat/KM of 16,000 M−1 s−1. A second set of 96 designs yielded three additional highly active enzymes, with reported maxima of 53,000 M−1 s−1 for kcat/KM and 1.5 s−1 for kcat. These are reported maxima and should not be assumed to describe the same enzyme without further evidence. The tested substrate was the fluorogenic ester 4-methylumbelliferyl phenylacetate, also identified as 4MU-PA.

The metallohydrolase authors also report that their RFdiffusion2–PLACER approach has yielded biocatalysts for a variety of bond-breaking and bond-making reactions in their laboratory. That statement indicates a broader author-reported scope than the highlighted ester demonstration. It neither demonstrates arbitrary-reaction capability nor supports restricting the field to only the two reactions described here. The supplied review does not establish the breadth, efficiency or process performance of those additional reactions.

These are dated Nature research results, rather than projections of the proposed general capability. According to the supplied review, the numerical account is supported by full article text. Some pages of the separate metallohydrolase PDF and certain associated PDFs lacked extractable text, but the intact article HTML supported the stated results; the underlying plots were not independently inspected in that review. This limits independent checking of graphical details without negating the text-supported measurements. The supplied record contains no freshness assessment establishing the latest field-wide position as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed generalization milestone: test a blinded panel spanning acid–base chemistry, hydrolysis, oxidation and carbon–carbon bond formation, including at least one reaction independently established to lack a useful catalyst within a defined search scope and set of operating conditions. Predefine the number of experimentally tested designs allowed per reaction, the permitted computational redesign rounds and the required coverage of the panel. Successful catalysts should emerge within that budget without a directed-evolution campaign. These panel and budget requirements are proposals for assessing the concept, not criteria prescribed by the supplied papers.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed generalization milestone

completion_criteria.text: A proposed kinetic target is to reach both kcat/KM of about 10^5 M−1 s−1 and kcat around 10 s−1 for successful panel reactions. These values are the median natural-enzyme benchmarks cited by Listov and colleagues, adopted here as a proposed reference point. They are not an established universal completion standard. Requiring both addresses distinct aspects of catalytic performance: activity relative to substrate concentration and turnover when substrate is saturating.
completion_criteria.label: A proposed kinetic target is to reach both

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: define reaction-specific requirements for product identity, selectivity, conversion and yield alongside kinetics. Measure performance at declared substrate concentrations and relevant temperature, pH and solvent conditions, and establish useful catalyst lifetime and product recovery where manufacturing is claimed. Report reagent, metal or cofactor requirements and any regeneration burden. The appropriate numerical thresholds should depend on the intended application and comparator process; the supplied evidence does not establish universal values for these requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope demonstration: independent laboratories should reproduce representative catalysts from disclosed sequences, preparation procedures and assay conditions. Report all tested designs and failures so that success rates and experimental costs can be assessed. Evaluate new, prospectively selected reaction requests after the initial panel, including substrates and mechanisms outside the original demonstrations. A finite panel would establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within its tested domain; it could not prove literal coverage of arbitrary reactions.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and scope demonstration

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-01, “A method that predicts realistic chemical outcomes before the experiment,” overlaps through the need to predict reaction pathways and competing outcomes. Prediction could help catalyst design, but predicting what happens does not by itself produce a catalyst. CHEMREV-04, “Practical, on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules,” could benefit from catalysts that enable otherwise inaccessible steps; it additionally requires route planning, execution and isolation of the requested molecule.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-06, “Mild nitrogen fixation that can compete with Haber–Bosch,” CHEMREV-11, “General, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond in a complex molecule,” and CHEMREV-12, “Selective conversion of methane to methanol at useful conversion under mild conditions,” are distinct possible application targets. A general catalyst designer would need to demonstrate each relevant transformation and its practical requirements. Success on any one of them would not establish general catalyst design, and the supplied Kemp-elimination and ester-hydrolysis studies establish none of these three capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-07, “A fossil-competitive primary supply of multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water,” and CHEMREV-13, “Commodity plastics returned to monomers at a cost and energy below virgin production,” could use advances in selective catalysis. Their defining outcomes also depend on complete process performance, including energy, feedstocks, separations and economics. Producing an active enzyme for an individual step would therefore be a possible contribution to either concept, rather than completion of it.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-02, “Open-ended Darwinian evolution in a synthetic chemical system,” concerns sustained evolutionary capacity in a chemical system. CHEMREV-05 concerns obtaining requested catalytic functions through design. Directed evolution can be a catalyst-development method, but that method is distinct from demonstrating open-ended synthetic evolution. The proposed completion panel for CHEMREV-05 deliberately tests performance without a directed-evolution campaign.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-09, “Phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids,” shares the challenge of translating a design into a reliably produced physical object, but its output is a crystalline material rather than a reaction catalyst. CHEMREV-10, “Positional chemical manufacture of macroscopic, atomically specified matter,” demands controlled assembly of specified matter; catalytic acceleration and selectivity alone do not supply that positional manufacturing capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-03, “A manufacturable room-temperature superconductor at ambient pressure,” and CHEMREV-08, “A rechargeable air-breathing battery with aviation-relevant specific energy,” have no direct enabling relationship established by the supplied catalyst evidence. Catalysts might contribute to particular material-production or battery processes, but neither superconductivity nor aviation-level battery performance follows from general enzyme design.

change_log.change: Preserved CHEMREV-05 and its original title while explaining the intended general capability separately from the demonstrated reaction-specific achievements.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even though the supplied evidence does not establish arbitrary-reaction capability.

change_log.change: Corrected the further Kemp variant to 123,000 M−1 s−1 and 30 s−1, named Phe113Leu, and retained the approximately 2.8 s−1 value for Des27.7 with the more precise results-text value.
change_log.reason: The review supports these measurements and identifies the earlier assertion of turnover above 30 s−1 as a narrow numerical error.

change_log.change: Added publication dates, the hydrolase substrate identity, both 96-design rounds and the distinction between reported maxima and a jointly established performance pair.
change_log.reason: These details clarify when, on what chemistry and at what experimental scope the achievements were demonstrated.

change_log.change: Distinguished experimental screening and computational redesign from a directed-evolution campaign.
change_log.reason: Avoiding directed evolution does not imply that successful catalysts were obtained without experimental selection or iteration.

change_log.change: Interpreted the introductory statement about elusive natural-level proficiency as historical context and included the hydrolase authors' broader laboratory-scope statement with attribution.
change_log.reason: Neither statement should erase the documented achievements or justify limiting accessible chemistry to the two highlighted reactions.

change_log.change: Qualified the field-wide inability claim and separated the dated demonstrations from the unverified position as of 1 November 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record is empty and cannot establish present-day openness.

change_log.change: Retained the manufacturing significance and hard-reaction examples as conditional implications, while removing categorical adoption and substitution claims.
change_log.reason: Catalytic kinetics alone do not establish industrial economics, process readiness or replacement of precious-metal processes.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include a predefined design budget, selectivity, process performance, reproducibility and prospective scope testing.
change_log.reason: A finite kinetic panel is a useful proposed generalization milestone but cannot establish literal universality or practical readiness.

change_log.change: Preserved PDF extraction and plot-inspection limitations while explaining the available full-HTML support.
change_log.reason: Partial extraction limits independent inspection without constituting evidence that the reported results are false.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to the supplied roster while keeping each innovation distinct and labeling uncited engineering and impact reasoning as synthesis or proposals.
change_log.reason: Shared enabling methods and possible applications do not make separate breakthrough goals equivalent.

unresolved_issues: The latest field-wide capability as of 1 November 2026 is unresolved because the supplied record contains no freshness assessment.
The breadth and performance of the additional bond-making and bond-breaking reactions mentioned by the hydrolase authors are not established in the supplied review.
The design budget, allowed iteration count and required panel success rate remain to be specified for the proposed blinded demonstration.
Reaction-specific selectivity, catalyst lifetime, process-condition and economic thresholds remain undefined.
The search scope and practical definition needed to establish that a panel reaction lacks a useful catalyst remain to be specified.

The supplied review did not independently inspect underlying plots, and some metallohydrolase-related PDF pages lacked extractable text; graphical details beyond the reviewed article text remain unchecked.
No supplied evidence demonstrates nitrogen fixation, methane-to-methanol conversion or chosen-site C–H functionalization using these workflows.
